June 15, 2026 
 
Re: Docket No. CMS-2026-1255 | Medicare and Medicaid Programs: Patient Protection and 
Affordable Care Act; Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs for Medicare 
Advantage Organizations, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, etc. 
 
ALS United appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services’ 
Request for Information regarding prior authorization and access to laboratory testing, as referenced in 
Section III.E of the proposed rule. 
  
ALS United is a nationwide partnership of independent nonprofit organizations dedicated to serving the 
ALS community through research, care, and advocacy. ALS is a fatal, progressive neurodegenerative 
disease that often moves quickly and leaves patients, families, and clinicians with little room for 
administrative delay. For people living with ALS, timely access to medically necessary laboratory testing 
is not a secondary or technical issue. It can affect diagnosis, treatment decisions, medication safety 
monitoring, access to genetically targeted therapies, and the ability to track disease progression. 
  
ALS United supports CMS’s broader efforts to modernize prior authorization and urges the agency to 
ensure that laboratory testing policies reflect the clinical realities of serious, progressive, and rare 
diseases. Prior authorization rules should not delay medically necessary testing, force redundant blood 
draws, deny coverage based on paperwork timing, or leave patients with unexpected financial liability 
when patients and clinicians acted in good faith. 
  
Summary of Recommendations 
  
ALS United respectfully urges CMS to: 
  
• 
Prohibit prior authorization denials based solely on the timing of specimen collection, 
particularly where the test was medically necessary and ordered by the treating clinician. 
• 
Prevent unnecessary repeat blood draws when a viable specimen is already available. 
• 
Protect patients from surprise bills, out-of-pocket costs, and coverage denials when 
administrative delays are outside the patient’s control.  
• 
Establish expedited review pathways for laboratory testing needed in serious, progressive, rare, 
or time-sensitive conditions, including ALS. 
• 
Ensure prior authorization policies do not create barriers to genetic testing, biomarker testing, 
medication safety monitoring, or other laboratory testing that is clinically relevant to ALS care. 
• 
Require payers to recognize appropriate clinical documentation from treating clinicians and 
laboratories to support medical necessity. 
• 
Allow appropriately documented retroactive authorization when specimens have already been 
collected and are clinically valid for testing. 
  
Laboratory Testing Plays an Increasingly Important Role in ALS Care 
  
ALS care is evolving. While there remains an urgent need for more effective therapies, advances in 
genetics, biomarkers, and targeted treatment approaches are making laboratory testing increasingly 
important for patients and clinicians. 
  
Genetic testing can help identify mutation-defined forms of ALS and determine whether a patient may 
be eligible for targeted therapies, clinical trials, or family counseling. In some cases, specialty laboratory 
tests related to genetic testing are not consistently covered by insurance or may be difficult to categorize 
as either clinical care or research. Coverage uncertainty and prior authorization barriers can leave 
patients and families caught between a clinical recommendation and an insurance process that does not 
reflect the realities of rare disease care. 
  
Biomarker testing is also becoming increasingly relevant. Many ALS centers are using neurofilament 
light chain testing as a marker associated with neuronal injury and disease progression. While NfL is not 
an absolute indicator and should not be treated as a substitute for clinical judgment, ALS clinicians 
increasingly view it as a potentially important tool for monitoring disease activity and response to 
certain therapies. This is particularly relevant for patients receiving Qalsody (tofersen) for SOD1-ALS 
and for patients with other rare genetic forms of ALS where clinicians may use biomarker trends to help 
understand whether treatment is affecting the underlying disease process. 
  
Prior authorization policies that delay, deny, or impose unnecessary administrative burdens on this 
testing can have real consequences. ALS is a rapidly progressive disease. A delay of weeks or months can 
materially affect whether a patient receives timely information about treatment options, progression, 
trial eligibility, or care planning. 
  
Medication Safety Monitoring Should Not Be Delayed or Denied 
  
Laboratory testing is also necessary for routine safety monitoring in ALS care. For example, liver function 
testing is commonly used during the first months of treatment with riluzole because the medication can 
increase liver enzymes, including ALT and AST. This monitoring is not experimental. It is part of 
responsible medication management. 
  
ALS United is concerned that some patients have been charged for routine liver function tests or required 
to appeal denials even when the testing was ordered for standard monitoring related to ALS therapy. 
These barriers are not minor administrative inconveniences. They can create financial stress, discourage 
adherence to appropriate monitoring, and place patients in the unfair position of choosing between 
paying out of pocket, delaying a test, or navigating an appeal while managing a progressive fatal disease. 
  
Prior Authorization Rules Must Align With Real-World Laboratory Workflows 
  
ALS United is particularly concerned by prior authorization policies that deny coverage because 
authorization was not finalized before or on the exact date a specimen was collected. In real-world care, 
a clinician may order testing, a specimen may be collected, and the laboratory may receive or process 
that specimen only after administrative steps are underway. When coverage turns on an arbitrary 
collection-date technicality, patients can be penalized for timing issues that are entirely outside their 
control. 
  
This creates several avoidable harms. A valid specimen may be rejected or discarded. A patient may be 
forced to undergo another blood draw. Testing results may be delayed. The treating clinician may lack 
information needed to make a timely care decision. The patient may face unexpected bills, appeals, and 
additional stress. 
  
For people living with ALS, repeat blood draws and additional clinic visits are not minor inconveniences. 
ALS can affect mobility, breathing, communication, swallowing, energy levels, and the ability to travel. 
Returning to a clinic may require caregiver support, accessible transportation, time away from work for 
family members, and additional physical strain. Policies that force redundant testing because of 
paperwork timing are especially inappropriate for patients with progressive neuromuscular disease. 
  
CMS Should Require Patient-Centered Protections 
  
ALS United urges CMS to require health plans to adopt prior authorization policies for laboratory testing 
that are aligned with clinical workflows and patient needs. 
  
First, CMS should prohibit timing-based denials when a medically necessary test was ordered by the 
treating clinician and the specimen was collected before the authorization process was completed. If the 
specimen is valid and the documentation supports medical necessity, coverage should not be denied 
solely because the authorization was pending on the collection date. 
  
Second, CMS should require payers to allow retroactive authorization for laboratory testing when the 
specimen has already been collected. This is particularly important for specialty laboratory testing, 
biomarker testing, and genetic testing, where specimens may be collected in one setting and processed 
by a different laboratory. 
  
Third, CMS should prohibit policies that force repeat blood draws when a valid specimen is already 
available. Patients should not undergo duplicative procedures solely to satisfy administrative 
sequencing requirements. 
  
Fourth, CMS should establish expedited review expectations for laboratory testing needed in serious, 
progressive, or rare diseases, including ALS. This should include testing used for treatment eligibility, 
safety monitoring, biomarker monitoring, genetic classification, and clinical trial evaluation. 
  
Finally, CMS should protect patients from financial liability when they, their clinicians, and the laboratory 
acted in good faith. Patients should not receive surprise bills or be forced into appeals because of delays 
or inconsistencies in payer prior authorization processes. 
  
Conclusion 
  
ALS United appreciates CMS’s attention to the impact of prior authorization on access to laboratory 
testing. For people living with ALS, laboratory testing can be essential to timely diagnosis, treatment 
planning, safety monitoring, biomarker assessment, and access to emerging targeted therapies. These 
tests should not be delayed or denied because of administrative timing rules that do not reflect how care 
is delivered. 
  
CMS should ensure that prior authorization policies support timely, medically necessary laboratory 
testing and protect patients from redundant procedures, avoidable delays, and unfair financial burdens. 
For people living with ALS and their families facing a rapidly progressive fatal disease, time matters. 
Prior authorization rules should not stand between patients and the clinical information their care 
teams need. 
  
Respectfully submitted, 
 
Jerry Dawson 
President and CEO 
ALS United

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** ALS United; signed by Jerry Dawson, President and CEO
- **Stakeholder type:** Advocacy Group
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Nationwide partnership of independent nonprofit organizations serving the ALS community through research, care, and advocacy.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

ALS United supports CMS's broader efforts to modernize prior authorization and asks CMS to ensure laboratory-testing prior authorization policies account for serious, progressive, rare, and time-sensitive diseases such as ALS. The comment focuses on patient-centered protections: no timing-only denials, no redundant blood draws when a valid specimen exists, expedited review for clinically urgent testing, retroactive authorization when appropriate, and protection from surprise bills caused by administrative delays.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** GENERAL; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PATIENT-ACCESS-related concerns under the broader prior authorization framework.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** None cited directly; comment references Section III.E of the proposed rule regarding prior authorization and laboratory testing.
- **Standards referenced:** No specific technical standards such as FHIR IGs or NCPDP are referenced.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Prior Authorization for Laboratory Testing in ALS and Rare Disease Care**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** ALS progresses rapidly and laboratory testing can affect diagnosis, treatment decisions, medication safety monitoring, genetically targeted therapies, clinical trial eligibility, and disease progression tracking.
- **Specific request:** Require PA policies for laboratory testing to reflect clinical workflows and patient needs, especially for serious, progressive, rare, or time-sensitive conditions.

**Topic 2: Timing-Based Denials and Retroactive Authorization**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Denials based solely on specimen collection date penalize patients for administrative sequencing outside their control and may delay clinically valid testing.
- **Specific request:** Prohibit denials based solely on specimen timing and allow documented retroactive authorization when specimens have already been collected and remain clinically valid.

**Topic 3: Redundant Specimen Collection and Patient Burden**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Requiring repeat blood draws for ALS patients can impose substantial physical, logistical, caregiver, transportation, and financial burdens.
- **Specific request:** Prohibit policies that force repeat blood draws when a viable specimen is already available.

**Topic 4: Expedited Review and Patient Financial Protection**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS / GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Delays of weeks or months can materially affect ALS treatment planning, genetic/biomarker information, medication safety monitoring, and clinical trial access.
- **Specific request:** Establish expedited review pathways for laboratory testing needed in serious, progressive, rare, or time-sensitive conditions and protect patients from bills or coverage denials when patients, clinicians, and laboratories acted in good faith.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S66-S82:** The comment responds to the general RFI area concerning prior authorization and laboratory testing, particularly how PA can affect access to tests needed for serious, progressive, rare, or time-sensitive conditions. ALS United recommends protections for timing-based denials, retroactive authorization, expedited review, and patient financial liability.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Prohibit PA denials based solely on the timing of specimen collection when a medically necessary test was ordered by the treating clinician.
2. Prevent unnecessary repeat blood draws when a viable specimen is already available.
3. Protect patients from surprise bills, out-of-pocket costs, and coverage denials caused by administrative delays beyond their control.
4. Establish expedited review pathways for laboratory testing needed in serious, progressive, rare, or time-sensitive conditions, including ALS.
5. Ensure PA policies do not block genetic testing, biomarker testing, medication safety monitoring, or other ALS-relevant laboratory testing.
6. Require payers to recognize appropriate clinical documentation from treating clinicians and laboratories.
7. Permit appropriately documented retroactive authorization when specimens have already been collected and remain clinically valid.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Administrative timing rules, delayed or denied laboratory testing, redundant blood draws, unexpected patient financial liability, and failure to account for ALS care realities.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Delayed diagnosis or treatment planning, lost access to targeted therapies or clinical trials, delayed safety monitoring, financial stress, additional physical burden, and avoidable appeals.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Real-world laboratory workflows in which ordering, specimen collection, lab receipt, processing, and authorization may not occur in the exact sequence required by payer rules.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** No numerical statistics cited.
- **Studies or research referenced:** None cited.
- **Examples provided:** Genetic testing for mutation-defined ALS; neurofilament light chain testing; Qalsody (tofersen) for SOD1-ALS; liver function testing for riluzole safety monitoring; repeat blood draws caused by authorization timing issues.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** ALS patients and families, treating clinicians, laboratories, payers, and rare disease care teams.
- **Economic implications:** Potential reduction in avoidable out-of-pocket costs, surprise bills, appeals, repeat testing, and redundant visits.
- **Technical feasibility:** Comment does not address FHIR/NCPDP implementation; feasibility focus is operational alignment with lab workflows and retroactive/expedited authorization processes.
- **Patient care impact:** High; timely testing affects diagnosis, treatment eligibility, biomarker monitoring, medication safety, clinical trial access, and disease progression management.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive with modifications
- **Tone:** Professional, patient-centered, urgent
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "For people living with ALS, timely access to medically necessary laboratory testing is not a secondary or technical issue." - Context: Establishing why lab testing access should be treated as clinically urgent.
2. "Prior authorization rules should not delay medically necessary testing, force redundant blood draws, deny coverage based on paperwork timing, or leave patients with unexpected financial liability when patients and clinicians acted in good faith." - Context: Summary of requested patient protections.
3. "When coverage turns on an arbitrary collection-date technicality, patients can be penalized for timing issues that are entirely outside their control." - Context: Objection to timing-based denials.
4. "For people living with ALS and their families facing a rapidly progressive fatal disease, time matters." - Context: Closing rationale for expedited and patient-centered policies.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - Requests expedited review pathways and objects to delays caused by administrative sequencing.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Highlights clinician and laboratory documentation burdens and appeals caused by PA rules.
- [x] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - Addresses protections for people with serious, progressive, rare diseases who face heightened consequences from delays.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Central theme; focuses on timely access to laboratory testing needed for diagnosis, treatment, monitoring, and trial eligibility.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Requests clearer documentation recognition and coverage protections so patients are not surprised by denials or bills.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Emphasizes that PA rules must align with real-world laboratory workflows and specimen processing.
